hints: Start from the R group change given in the stem. What is the difference in chemical character between glutamine and valine, and where on the haemoglobin molecule does this new group sit?
Think about how a new exposed surface group changes bonding. What type of bonds could now form not within one molecule but between neighbouring Hb molecules at low $p\mathrm{O}_2$?
walkthrough:
Link Mutation to Primary Structure**
You have a single base substitution that swaps one amino acid for another. That means the sequence - the primary structure - is altered. Here polar glutamine with a hydrophilic R group is replaced by valine with a hydrophobic non-polar R group on the surface of the beta-globin chain.

From New R Group to Fibres**
A surface hydrophobic patch does not like water, so at low $p\mathrm{O}_2$ when haemoglobin is deoxygenated it fits into a hydrophobic pocket on a neighbouring HbS molecule. Many such bonds between molecules make them stick together and polymerise into long fibres that distort the red cell.

Final answer: The substitution changes the primary structure from polar glutamine to non-polar valine. The non-polar valine R groups form different hydrophobic bonds between adjacent HbS molecules, so they stick together to form fibres.

hints: Compare the adult haemoglobin mixture with and without British-198. What percentage of HbF remains, and what special property of HbF at low $p\mathrm{O}_2$ is given in the bullet points?
Connect that property to fibre formation. If oxygen stays bound longer and HbS molecules are diluted by HbF, what happens to sickling and capillary blocking?
walkthrough:
More HbF Persists**
Normally HbF falls to less than 1% by six months. With British-198 it stays around 20% in the adult, so red cells contain both HbF and HbS together.

Less Sickling**
HbF binds oxygen more strongly at low $p\mathrm{O}_2$, helping avoid the very low $p\mathrm{O}_2$ that triggers sickling, and HbF molecules get in the way of HbS-HbS joining. That stops or greatly reduces fibre formation, so fewer cells become sickle shaped and fewer capillaries are blocked, giving milder symptoms.

Final answer: With British-198 adults retain up to 20% HbF with HbS. HbF has higher affinity for oxygen at low $p\mathrm{O}_2$ and disrupts HbS fibre formation, so fewer red cells sickle and block capillaries.

hints: Recall the general name for any protein that binds DNA to switch a gene on or off by controlling transcription.
walkthrough:
Naming the Control Protein**
Genes for fetal globin are switched on and off by proteins that bind to DNA near the gene and control whether RNA polymerase can transcribe it. The standard syllabus term for such a gene-switching protein is a transcription factor, also accepted as a regulatory protein.

hints: Picture the gel set-up. What electrical condition is applied across the gel, and in which direction will negatively charged haemoglobin molecules move?
All molecules are made negative by alkaline pH, but HbS is given as more positive than HbA. How will that affect its net charge and speed?
Translate speed difference into position on the gel after the same time. Which band will be closer to the start?
Think how you decide a diagnosis from bands. What must you compare the test sample with, and what pattern means all haemoglobin is HbS?
walkthrough:
Set Up the Field and Movement**
Samples are loaded in wells and a current creates a potential difference across the gel. In alkaline buffer all haemoglobin molecules carry a net negative charge, so they are attracted through the gel matrix toward the positive electrode, the anode.

Why HbS Lags Behind**
HbS has an additional positive charge compared with HbA, so its net negative charge is smaller. A smaller net charge means a weaker pull to the anode, so HbS migrates more slowly and after the run sits a shorter distance from the negative end than HbA.

Reading the Diagnosis**
You run reference haemoglobins HbA, HbF and HbS alongside the test, often in lane 5. Matching the test band positions to the references identifies which haemoglobins are present. A person with sickle cell anaemia makes only HbS, so you see a single band at the HbS position, while carriers show two bands.

Final answer: Apply a p.d. / electric field across the gel; negatively charged haemoglobins move toward the anode / positive electrode. HbS is more positive so less negative overall and moves more slowly / shorter distance from the negative end. Compare band positions to known HbA, HbF, HbS references; a single band at the HbS position indicates sickle cell anaemia.

hints: Use lane 1 (normal adult, HbA only) and lane 5 (HbA, HbF, HbS reference) as rulers. What haemoglobins would a one-month-old normal baby still contain, and what two haemoglobins must a HbA/HbS heterozygote make?
For sickle cell anaemia all adult haemoglobin is HbS. How many bands will that give and at which reference level will it sit?
walkthrough:
Work Out Each Genotype and Age**
Lane 1 shows a normal adult has only the top HbA band. A one-month-old normal baby has not yet switched fully, so still has much HbF plus HbA. An SCT person is heterozygous HbA/HbS so makes both normal and sickle beta chains. A sickle cell anaemia person is homozygous HbS/HbS so makes only HbS.

Place the Bands Against the Reference**
Match to lane 5 where top to bottom is HbA, HbF, HbS. Draw in lane 2 two bands at HbA and HbF levels, in lane 3 two bands at HbA and HbS levels, and in lane 4 one band only at the lowest HbS level.
Final answer: Lane 2 (one-month-old normal): bands at HbA and HbF positions. Lane 3 (SCT heterozygote): bands at HbA and HbS positions. Lane 4 (sickle cell anaemia): single band at HbS position only.
